Could another 1859 Carrington event fail to be detected ?

No. We have quite an extensive network of magnetometers, ionospheric observations systems, satellites monitoring solar wind and flares etc. There is absolutely no possible way it would go unnoticed. Regardless of multiple scientific observation systems, there would probably be quite a lot of effects observable in day to day life (aurora, radio interference, possibly failing of satellites like GPS etc.).

The somewhat more interesting question, surprisingly, is whether such an event has already been detected since. Because the observations at the time were not done according to modern standards, there are some scientist who suggest that the 1989 (Quebec Blackout storm) or 1941 (The Playoffs Storm) events might have been of the same order. It is not entirely clear how the 1859 event would have been registered by modern instruments.

According to the article:

In 1859 the largest and most powerful solar storm ever recorded, also known as the Carrington Event or the Carrington Flare in honour of the English Astronomer Richard Carrington who observed it, was detected at the Colaba Observatory in India. This solar storm allowed for the observation of auroras at latitudes as low as Madrid and even the Caribbean Sea. However, the storm was also the cause of power outages and fires at telegraph system facilities all over Europe and North America.

One of the conclusions is that the indices commonly used by scientists -such as Dst or SYM-H, which are based on an overall perspective of the Earth and obtained by calculating averages,- failed to detect such an important event, and they most likely would have failed to detect the Carrington Event as well," explains Consuelo Cid, the lead author.

So yep, we could miss the next solar disturbance that could destroy our power and communications grid.
